h1: Calypso hops for apple and pear notes in a pale ale
title: Calypso Hops: Apple and Pear Notes | Craft Beer School
desc: What Calypso hops taste like and why they smell of apple and pear. How a home brewer can use them in a pale ale without losing the fruit.
teaser: Most hops promise grapefruit. Calypso smells of orchard fruit. It is easy to waste.
standfirst: Calypso is an American hop with a green apple, pear and stone fruit aroma, with a touch of lime. In a pale ale it makes a beer that smells like a fruit bowl. Here is how to keep that character.
sections: The hop that smells like an orchard

Calypso is an American dual purpose hop. Most citrus hops push grapefruit and orange. Calypso leans the other way, towards apple, pear and a hint of stone fruit, with a little lime in the background. Its alpha acids sit around 12 to 16%, which is high enough to bitter a beer and still leaves a good oil load for aroma.

That makes it a clear teaching hop. If you want to understand what an aroma hop contributes, brew a beer where Calypso is the only late addition and the fruit you taste is its own. A bland pale malt base and a neutral yeast are the right partners, because anything with its own character muddies the experiment.

Calypso also sits in a wider family of American hops that moved brewing beyond Cascade-style grapefruit. Our American hops guide sets out how that happened.
A simple pale ale to show it off

For 20 L, mash 3.8 kg of pale malt and 200 g of light crystal malt at 66 to 67 °C for 60 minutes. That gives a starting gravity near 1.050 and a fairly dry finish. Bitter with about 15 g of Calypso at 60 minutes for roughly 25 IBU, with the whirlpool adding a little more, then keep the rest of the hop for late.

Chill the wort to 80 °C, add 40 g of Calypso and stand for 20 minutes. Cool the rest of the way and pitch a clean ale yeast at 18 to 19 °C. Dry hop with another 40 g for three days at the end of fermentation. Choose a neutral yeast: fruity English strains will compete with the hop.
Why the aroma fades in the wrong hands

Hop aroma is carried by essential oils. Oils are volatile. A long hard boil removes them. Adding aroma hops at 10 minutes or less, or in a whirlpool below 80 °C, keeps more of what you paid for.

Fruit esters in hops are also delicate once the beer is made. Oxygen takes them first. When you dry hop, keep the lid on, purge the fermenter with CO2 if you can and avoid long gaps with the fermenter open. A homebrew that smells wonderful on day three and flat on day thirty has usually lost its aroma to oxygen.

Temperature matters too. Dry hopping at 15 to 20 °C extracts oil faster than fridge temperature, but it also pulls grassy, vegetal notes if the pellets sit for a week. Three days is a good starting point. Taste a sample each day if you can spare it. Cold crash when the apple note peaks.

Calypso does well alongside hops with similar softness. Pair it with Amarillo for orange and flowers, or Palisade for apricot. Fruitier tropical hops such as El Dorado can swamp the apple note, so keep them to a minor share.

Keep the hop bill short. Two or three varieties are enough. A single variety teaches you the most.

Keep the malt simple as well: a pale base and a little crystal at most. Biscuit or roasted grains cover soft fruit notes. This is why many brewers use a plain pale ale as the test bed for any new hop before they spend it on something stronger.

Hop pellets are imported and sold in small packs for homebrewers. Keep them in the freezer, in a sealed bag with the air pressed out. Warm, humid kitchens age pellets fast.

Fermenting a pale ale in an Indian summer without temperature control is the larger risk to hop flavour. Above about 24 °C a clean ale yeast makes fusel notes and fruity esters that cover the hop. A fermenter in a tub of water with a wet towel and a fan can hold it several degrees cooler. A fridge with an external controller is better still.

Finally, write down what you did. Hop weights, times, temperatures and the day you tasted each sample are cheap to record and expensive to forget. A notebook or a simple spreadsheet is enough. When the second batch tastes different from the first, the notes tell you why. That habit is the difference between brewing a good beer once and brewing it on demand.
faqs: What does Calypso hop taste like?
Green apple and pear with stone fruit and a little lime. It is gentler than grapefruit hops.
It can be, with alpha acids around 12 to 16%, but most brewers keep it for aroma because that is where its character shows.
Can I use Calypso in a lager?
Yes, in a pale lager or a hoppy lager if you want fruit, but keep the fermentation clean and cold, between 8 and 13 °C, so the fruit comes from the hop.
